mn_01: How one three seven makes money — the whole thinking, start to finish. We ran the pricing question hard: dozens of models, the legal wall around them, a sharp outside critique, and the challenge back. This is all of it, in order. The short version — we price the firm's access to organizing capacity, and we never, ever price the case.
mn_02: Here is the one idea everything else serves. We monetize the firm's software, configuration, and processing capacity — and we keep the price completely independent from whether a worker signs, is accepted, or wins. Price the capacity to organize. Never the outcome of a matter. Say that until it is reflex.
mn_03: First, the wall — the things we can never charge for, no matter how much money is sitting there. Never a percentage of a recovery. Never a fee per signed case or per retainer. Never a fee per lead. And never a referral fee for sending a worker to a firm. Every one of those is where legal's money visibly sits, and every one is barred to us.
mn_04: That wall is not a cage — it is the advantage. Every competitor prices on the case: the lead, the signing, the settlement. We are forbidden from standing on that ground, so we are forced into the one place nobody in legal bothers to look — pricing the capacity to organize. The alley is empty because everyone else is allowed to stay on the main road. We are not. So we found the alley.
mn_05: Now the correction that matters most, because it is easy to get wrong. There is not one legal rule here — there are two, and they ask different questions. Section six one five five asks: are we a lawyer referral service? Rule five point four asks: are we sharing in a legal fee? Confuse them, and you will guard the wrong door.
mn_06: Section six one five five is about routing. Do we rank, match, prefer, or steer a worker toward a particular firm? If the worker independently chooses the firm — and can build and export their record with us not involved at all — we are a tool the worker uses, not a service that refers them. The billing unit does not move this needle. Routing does.
mn_07: Rule five point four is about outcome-linkage. Does our money follow the win? This is the rule that actually bars charging per signed case or a share of a recovery — because that is sharing in the legal fee. So the discipline is simple: our price may never move because a case was accepted, settled, or won.
mn_08: So here is the truth about the meter — the thing we charge per. The meter matters for exactly two things: rule five point four, never tie it to an outcome; and our own roster tripwire, meter tool use, not clients delivered. The meter does not make us a referral service — routing does. So do not burn the legal budget arguing what to call the unit. Spend it proving the worker chooses the firm.
mn_09: This reframes the free worker side. Everyone treats free-for-workers as an adoption tactic. It is far more than that — it is the load-bearing compliance wall. If a worker can complete and walk away with their record without any firm ever involved, we are infrastructure the worker controls, not a marketplace that places them. Free, exportable, and firm-optional is not generosity. It is the foundation that keeps us legal.
mn_10: We generated dozens of pricing models and scored them hard. The strong ones all clustered in the same place: free worker access, firms paying for capacity and seats, element-packs that expand use, and annual prepay with a founding-firm offer. The weak and the dead ones all reached for the case. The signal was loud and clear.
mn_11: The hidden alley, then, is not a clever trick. It is this: price the firm's access to organizing capacity, and let the free worker side do the customer acquisition. Workers walk their organized file to the firm — distribution the firm never paid for. The firm buys the software to receive and work what walks in. That is the whole engine.
mn_12: The strongest commercial frame for capacity is reserved lanes — a firm buys the ability to have, say, ten intakes organizing at once, like reserved lanes on a road. It meters use, not cases, and it scales fairly. But here is the honest caveat: counsel must confirm it reads as capacity, not a disguised per-case meter. And a small firm may simply ask — why not just sell me a monthly allowance? Which brings us to the trap.
mn_13: The trap is thinking a monthly allowance is safer than lanes. It is not. If one intake uses one unit of allowance, an allowance is a per-matter meter wearing a cardigan — the exact same substance you were trying to avoid. You cannot escape per-matter substance by renaming it. There are only two honest exits: pure seats or a flat tier with no volume meter at all; or own one volume meter openly and manage how a unit is released. Pick one. Do not pretend a rename is a solution.
mn_14: For growth, element-packs are the cleanest expansion. Wage-and-hour is the base; PAGA, WARN, discrimination, and later other verticals are add-on packs. It expands how much of the platform a firm uses — never the economics of any case — and it turns our own doctrine, the element sets, into the thing we price. Land, then expand, without ever touching an outcome.
mn_15: Now framing — same money, better words. Do not lead with dollars per month. Lead with the labor you delete. Priced below the cost of one typical staff hour per available intake. Phrase it as a comparison, not a promise, unless a firm's real numbers back it. And the State Bar's own twenty twenty-six rule forces contingency firms to see A I as absorbed overhead — so avoided cost is the only lens they are even allowed to use.
mn_15b: And know the wallet you are pricing into. A firm's total legal-tech budget runs about eight to seventeen thousand dollars per attorney a year, and the slice specifically for A I and automated intake is roughly eighteen hundred to forty-five hundred per attorney — a hundred to two hundred fifty dollars per seat, per month. Those are illustrative industry benchmarks, so verify them. But they tell you the envelope: our lanes and packs have to land comfortably inside that A I line — and set against the paralegal hours we delete, they do.
mn_16: The second frame is sharper still, but say it carefully. Firms already pay for every lead whether it signs or not. We do not promise more signings — that is a result we cannot guarantee. We promise this: the firm reaches its own screening decision with far less reconstruction, so the no's get cheaper and faster. Price the cost of the declines they are already paying for. Faster no's, yes. More yeses, never a promise.
mn_17: One phrase to retire: reserve your lane in the network. It sounds great, and it is dangerous. Reserve, network, worker choice, and paid firm access, all together, sound exactly like paying for placement in a marketplace — the referral-service reading we must avoid. Capacity is fine. Network placement is not. Watch the branding as closely as the billing.
mn_18: We took a hard outside critique, and four of its corrections we adopted outright. Founding pricing is a defined term — twenty-four to thirty-six months — not lifetime. Source-linking is core trust, and never a premium tier. The counsel review is about architecture, not word choice. And we stopped overstating what section six one five five forbids — it regulates referral behavior, not every billing unit. A good critique makes the thesis stronger.
mn_19: But guard against the opposite failure too. Be infrastructure, not a marketplace — yes. Taken too far, that fear neuters the very thing that feeds us: the worker walking their file to a firm they chose. A worker who independently chooses a firm and sends their own record is not a marketplace transaction, even though a firm paid for the software that received it. The line is not never route. The line is: the worker chooses, we transmit, we never rank or prefer. Do not let caution build a compliant product with no distribution.
mn_20: So the spine we put in front of counsel is this. Free worker side. Firms buy software access with a capacity meter. Element-packs expand the account. Annual prepay. A capped founding offer. And no unit ever touches a case, a client, or an outcome. And counsel reviews the architecture, not the copy: does the worker or one three seven choose the firm? Do paying firms get any preferential visibility? Can the worker build and export with no firm at all? What exactly triggers a charge? Does any price move on retention, signing, or recovery? And do we ever receive a share of a legal fee?
mn_21: That is the whole of it. The safest competitive advantage was never a clever name for a billable unit. It is making one three seven genuinely function as worker-controlled record infrastructure — free in the worker's hands, priced only as software in the firm's. Price the capacity to organize. Never the case. Everything else is detail.
